newsitem.title: USA: Governors compromise on welfare immigrant cutoff.
newsitem.headline: Governors compromise on welfare immigrant cutoff.

text.p: U.S. governors said on Sunday they would work with Congress to protect elderly and disabled immigrants who will lose federal aid under a new welfare law, but backed away from recommending specific policy changes.

Papering over a deep split among state executives, the National Governors' Association worked out a compromise policy at its winter meeting, calling on Congress and the White House to aid legal immigrants -- without reopening the welfare law.

The vague language was approved by a NGA committee in place of an original proposal specifically stating that elderly and disabled immigrants who were in the United States before the law took effect should remain eligible for federal Food Stamps and disability aid.

Republican governors, under pressure from congressional Republican leaders, balked at the idea of reopening the welfare law less than six months after it was signed into law by President Clinton. The Republican Governors' Association voted on Saturday to oppose any reopening of the law.

"There are so many people who want to try to somehow suggest that the governors are already, merely months or even weeks into the new reform act, getting nervous," said Michigan Republican Gov. John Engler. "We've got to guard against that."
Republican governors took the lead last year in asking Congress for more power under the new welfare law -- although they were never able to agree on the issue of immigrants.

The face-saving compromise, which must still be adopted by the full NGA, in effect says governors agree the welfare law's immigrant provisions will hurt some states. But it enables Republicans to say they did not seek to revamp the law.
Governors of affected states said they were happy the NGA was willing to at least admit there was a problem. Hundreds of thousands of immigrants will begin losing benefits in coming months.
"When this hits the fan ... in my state and other states I certainly want to be on record as telling them this was a bad policy," said Florida Democratic Gov. Lawton Chiles.

Possible options to address the issue included setting up a special fund to aid states like Texas, California, Florida and New York with large immigrant populations. An estimated 100,000 immigrants could be affected in Florida alone.
Clinton's 1998 budget, to be sent to Congress on Thursday, includes funding to restore aid to legal immigrants.

California Republican Gov. Pete Wilson said he was hopeful Congress would work out a solution, adding that Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott, who worked to tone down the NGA policy, worried about providing more money for immmigrants.
"He's willing to work with us in a way that will be responsive. Obviously, there's a concern on his part with respect to the money that is involved," Wilson said.

The immigrant cutoff saves $24 billion over six years -- more than 40 percent of the savings in the welfare law. Lott, who wants the savings to help balance the budget, says states have built up budget surpluses and should be able to address the problem.

The governors on Sunday also called for "technical" changes to the welfare law, including altering some work requirements and ensuring a five-year time limit on welfare applies only to cash aid and not other benefits.

The governors also reiterated their opposition to any federal spending cap on the Medicaid health program for 37 million poor, elderly and disabled, saying it would result in a huge cost shift to the states.
Clinton's budget is expected to include spending limits on Medicaid, jointly funded by state and local governments.

President Clinton's Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles, who spoke to the governors on Sunday, said the White House was committed to controlling growth in Medicaid, which compromises about 20 percent of state budgets on average.
